solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Note by note, old lady pockets old currency (10)

indicatorNotes.pockets: the old lady puts the currency in her pocket, so MUM goes round O RAND

blocks.note: ME (or MI) is the third note of the sol-fa scale
one's old lady is one's mother
O is the standard abbreviation for old
the rand is South Africa's currency

annotation.surface: An elderly woman has squirrelled away some obsolete money, a note at a time.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Old currency' looks like one pre-decimal coin but splits in two, and the old lady is a mother, pocketing both pieces.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a memo, the short form, is a written note or reminder.

entries.clue: Cut off, beheaded, Chancellor canonised from now on (8)

indicatorNotes.beheaded: a word with its head cut off loses its first letter

blocks.note: SEVER (cut off) without its first letter
Sir Thomas More, Henry VIII's Lord Chancellor, was made a saint in 1935

annotation.surface: A Tudor Chancellor is beheaded and made a saint for ever after, which is what happened to Thomas More.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface tells More's own story: Henry VIII had him beheaded, and the Church later canonised him.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the word means for ever, always from this moment onward.

entries.clue: Back of folio paper frequently used by poets (3)

indicatorNotes.Back of: the back of a word is its last letter

blocks.note: last letter of FOLIO
FT is the Financial Times, a newspaper

annotation.surface: Poets often write on the reverse of a folio sheet.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Paper' is a newspaper, not writing paper, and 'used by poets' is part of the definition: OFT is a poetic word.
annotation.definitionFit: A literary form: the old poetic word for often.

entries.clue: Book ultimately unfinished (5)

indicatorNotes.unfinished: a word left unfinished loses its last letter

blocks.note: ultimately = at last; 'unfinished' then drops its final T

annotation.surface: A book that was never completed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Ultimately' is a phrase in disguise, AT LAST, and cutting its end gives ATLAS.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a bound collection of maps is one kind of book.

entries.clue: CID officers placed last in the contest (7)

indicatorNotes.last in: the last letter in the word that follows

blocks.note: DIs are Detective Inspectors of the CID, the British police's plain-clothes branch
placed = put
last letter of THE

annotation.surface: The detectives came last in some competition.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Contest' looks like a noun in the surface; here it is the verb, as in to dispute a claim.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for the verb: to argue against a claim or result.

entries.clue: Doctor to Arab trapped in an upsetting obsession (9)

indicatorNotes.trapped in: OMANI is shut inside the letters that follow
indicatorNotes.upsetting: in a down clue, upsetting turns a word upside down, so AN reads NA

blocks.note: MO is a Medical Officer
AN turned upside down
someone from Oman

annotation.surface: A doctor treats an Arab patient caught in a distressing fixation.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Arab' is specific here: an Omani, which then sits inside a flipped AN.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a fixation on one single subject, the MONO- part meaning one.

entries.clue: Egg on curry goes oddly unnoticed (4)

indicatorNotes.oddly unnoticed: the odd-numbered letters are ignored, leaving the even ones

blocks.note: the 2nd, 4th, 6th and 8th letters of CURRY GOES

annotation.surface: Nobody notices an egg sitting on top of a curry, which is odd.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Egg on' looks like food on a plate; it is the verb meaning to encourage.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: to egg someone on is to push or encourage them into doing something.

entries.clue: After fiddling dad, our uncle is in disgrace (5,1,5)

indicatorNotes.fiddling: fiddling with letters meddles with their order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 11 letters

annotation.surface: Our uncle was caught fiddling Dad's money and is now in the family's bad books.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fiddling' reads as cheating, which fits the disgrace; its crossword job is to scramble the letters.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: someone out of favour or under suspicion is said to be in this state.

entries.clue: Channel crossing finally complete (6)

indicatorNotes.finally: the final letter of the word before

blocks.note: last letter of CROSSING
complete = utter, as in an utter fool

annotation.surface: A cross-Channel voyage has at last been completed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Channel crossing' paints the English Channel; the definition is a channel for water, and 'crossing' only supplies its last letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a trough along a roof or road edge that carries rainwater away.

entries.clue: Words of encouragement kept pals playing (3,5)

indicatorNotes.playing: the letters are at play, moving about

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters

annotation.surface: Some encouraging words kept a group of friends in the game.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Kept pals playing' reads as friends kept at a game; 'playing' is the only instruction, telling you to rearrange the two words before it.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: short rousing speeches, as a coach gives before a match.

entries.clue: Latest song heard in the raw state? (6)

indicatorNotes.heard: what is heard is spoken, so the sound counts, not the spelling

blocks.note: latest = NEW and song = DITTY; say the two together

annotation.surface: Someone is listening to the newest track while naked.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a pun: 'in the raw' means naked, so the raw state is nakedness.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: 'in the raw' means naked, so the raw state is being unclothed.

entries.clue: Small coat with singular cuffs (6)

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
a mack (or mac) is a mackintosh, a raincoat
S is the grammatical abbreviation for singular

annotation.surface: A small coat with unusual cuffs on its sleeves.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cuffs' looks like the ends of sleeves, and 'singular' like 'odd'; cuffs are blows here, and singular is just S.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for the verb: to cuff is to strike with the open hand.

entries.clue: Regularity of texture (11)

blocks.note: steadiness, being the same every time
how thick or smooth a sauce or paste is

annotation.surface: A fabric or food with an even texture.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one phrase, but it is two meanings of one word, joined by 'of'.
annotation.definitionFit: Two plain senses: steadiness of behaviour, and the thickness of a substance.

entries.clue: Classy uniform, rating’s favourite clothing (8)

indicatorNotes.clothing: PET clothes MARK: it wraps round it

blocks.note: U is Uniform in the NATO alphabet
the teacher's pet is the favourite
a rating is a mark or score

annotation.surface: A smart uniform that a sailor likes best to wear.
annotation.walkthrough: A rating is also a naval rank, a sailor, which is why 'uniform' feels natural; here it means a mark.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: expensive and aimed at wealthier customers.

entries.clue: A concern as it spread across the pond (12)

indicatorNotes.spread: the letters are spread out and laid down again in a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 12 letters

annotation.surface: A company grows until it has branches on the other side of the Atlantic.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The pond' is jokey British slang for the Atlantic, so across it is transoceanic.
annotation.definitionFit: A slang use: the pond is the Atlantic, and crossing an ocean is what the answer describes.

entries.clue: Command of weapons protecting India (9)

indicatorNotes.protecting: ORDNANCE surrounds I as a guard would

blocks.note: ordnance is military weapons and ammunition
I is India in the NATO alphabet

annotation.surface: Control over an arsenal that guards India.
annotation.walkthrough: ORDNANCE and ORDINANCE differ by one letter, and that I is exactly what the wordplay supplies.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: an authoritative order or decree.

entries.clue: Refuse to go in this bay aboard ship (3,5)

indicatorNotes.aboard: in a down clue BIN is placed on board, on top of, the ship

blocks.note: a bin is a storage bay or compartment, as for wine in a cellar
an ocean liner

annotation.surface: Someone declines to go into a bay on board a ship.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Refuse' reads as a verb, to decline; it is the noun, rubbish, and the bin liner is what it goes in.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: the plastic bag lining a rubbish bin is where refuse goes.

entries.clue: Italian team visiting a country’s state capital (12)

indicatorNotes.visiting: a visitor goes inside, so NAPOLI goes inside INDIA'S

blocks.note: INDIA'S, a country's
Napoli, the football club of Naples

annotation.surface: An Italian football side is visiting some nation's capital city.
annotation.walkthrough: 'State' looks like a nation, matching 'country'; it is a US state.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: it is the capital of the US state of Indiana.

entries.clue: Definite one’s the leader? (7)

blocks.note: read 'the' as a word: it is the definite one of its grammatical kind
a leader is also a newspaper's opinion piece, the leading item in the paper

annotation.surface: Someone asks whether a certain person is definitely in charge.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The leader' sounds like a person in charge; 'the' is the definite article, and a newspaper leader is the leading article.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses meet: 'the' is the definite article, and a newspaper leader is a leading article.

entries.clue: Is training able to accommodate a tasty morsel? (6)

indicatorNotes.to accommodate: CAN and PE together make room for A between them

blocks.note: able = can
PE is physical education, school sports training
the letter A

annotation.surface: A question whether exercise lets you fit in a little treat.
annotation.walkthrough: The wordplay reads 'training able', PE and CAN, housing A; the answer puts CAN first, then A, then PE.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a small savoury snack served with drinks.

entries.clue: One keen on discipline in term, a worrying time (8)

indicatorNotes.worrying: worrying at letters tugs them out of order

blocks.note: IN TERM A rearranged
T is the abbreviation for time

annotation.surface: A strict teacher makes the school term a stressful time.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In term' looks like a place in the school year; IN is part of the letters to rearrange.
annotation.definitionFit: An eponym: a stickler for discipline, named after Jean Martinet, a strict 17th-century French drillmaster.

entries.clue: Drake’s action heading off silly gossip (6)

indicatorNotes.heading off: the head, the first letter, goes

blocks.note: TWADDLE (silly gossip) without its first letter

annotation.surface: Sir Francis Drake takes action to stop foolish rumours.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Drake' suggests the Elizabethan sea captain; it is a male duck, whose walk is a waddle.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a drake is a male duck, and a duck's gait is this rolling walk.

entries.clue: Creep undermining women’s golf club (5)

indicatorNotes.undermining: in a down clue, EDGE goes under W

blocks.note: W is the abbreviation for women
to edge is to creep forward slowly

annotation.surface: A sneak is undermining a ladies' golf club.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Golf club' reads as a members' club; it is the stick, a wedge.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a golf club with a steeply angled face.

entries.clue: Outspoken cleric shot in the billiard room (6)

indicatorNotes.Outspoken: spoken out loud, so the word is judged by its sound

blocks.note: a canon is a clergyman of a cathedral

annotation.surface: A plain-speaking clergyman is shot dead in the billiard room, like a scene from Cluedo.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a murder mystery; a cannon is a billiards shot in which the cue ball hits two others.
annotation.definitionFit: A technical sense: in billiards, a shot where the cue ball strikes two balls in turn.

entries.clue: Rogue about to pass coursework? (8)

blocks.note: a cad is a rogue
to pass away is to die

annotation.surface: A rogue student is about to get a pass for their coursework.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Coursework' is school assignments in the surface; the question mark flags work on a golf course, carrying clubs.
annotation.definitionFit: A punning definition: carrying a golfer's clubs is work done on the golf course.

entries.clue: The old model made by Ford even now (3)

blocks.note: YE is the old form of THE, as in Ye Olde Shoppe
the Model T was Ford's famous car

annotation.surface: An old car model that Ford still makes today.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Model made by Ford' is the car, reduced to its letter; 'The old' is the mock-antique form seen on shop signs.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: still, up to this moment, as in 'not finished yet'.

entries.clue: Actual courage with no upfront support (4)

indicatorNotes.with no upfront: the support is removed from the front of the word

blocks.note: courage = bravery
a bra is a supporting garment, removed from the front

annotation.surface: Real bravery shown without any backing from the front line.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Actual' needs the old adjective sense, as in 'the very man', meaning the actual one.
annotation.definitionFit: An adjective sense: actual or exact, as in 'the very thing I wanted'.

entries.clue: Lead perhaps with a line that’s easy (10)

blocks.note: lead is a chemical element; 'perhaps' marks it as one example
the letter A
RY is short for railway, a line

annotation.surface: Taking the lead with a simple line.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lead' reads as leading the way; it is the metal. RY for railway is a standard crossword abbreviation.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: basic and simple, as in Sherlock Holmes's 'Elementary, my dear Watson'.
